content:
Thank you everyone for a great competition! I am sure we had a lot of fun exhausting a lot of FLOPs to run those crazy expensive Einsums!

Each team member ran their own pipeline independently without much sharing, to improve the diversity. I think this was crucial for us avoiding local optimas!

Jacek’s work

My workflow changed over time:

  • started with Claude Code 5x only
  • then I realized that ChatGPT 5.5 Pro Extended manages to solve more complex tasks that were too difficult to solve by Claude Code from scratch
  • at some point I switched from Claude Code to Codex
  • I started running multiple ChatGPT sessions in parallel and only use Codex to:
    • do local verification, identify slow and risky solutions, send solutions to kaggle to confirm
    • chase easier wins like transfer some new technique to other similar tasks or optimize runtime

I managed to achieve top2 on leaderboard while still going solo and then I teamed up. That meant adjusting the workflow and starting using our HF space to manage / monitor solutions.

I also tried to take advantage of everything that I learned in CodeGolf competition one year ago including knowledge about:

  • similar tasks
  • tasks with edge cases
  • manually created families of tasks

I used codegolf solutions as reference when solving tasks from scratch in early stage. It usually helped to get working solution faster, For complex tasks I usually manually curated a couple of reference solutions because hardcoded, regex, brute force or recursive ones didn't translate cleanly to ONNX graphs. But there was also downside: codegolf solutions were optimized for code length and that didn't translate to smaller graph, so I later removed all reference solutions from repository and only used generator and test samples to infer rules.

I kept track of all techniques in TECHNIQUES.md, at the end of the competition this file contained around 50k lines. It probably became too big at some point, I should have paid more attention to keep it clean.

Example 1:

fp32-underflow-threshold-classifier (use subnormal rounding as a strict count threshold)

Status: risky-probe

When to apply. A generator guarantees a tiny integer feature has a unique target threshold, e.g. one colour count is exactly 3 and every other colour count is at most 2. If the final verifier only checks output > 0, choose a small fp32 scale so values below the threshold underflow to +0.0 while the target value rounds to the smallest positive subnormal.

Recipe (from task129 updated_3):

# For legal counts c in {0,1,2,3}, choose SCALE so:
#   (2*SCALE)**2 -> +0.0, (3*SCALE)**2 -> min positive subnormal.
SCALE = np.float32(1.272753324395379e-23)
n("Einsum", ["input", "scale", "input", "scale", "input"], ["output"],
  equation="noab,e,nocd,e,ndhw->nohw")

Example 2 (discovered by Jin Niu)

static-rnn-relu-recurrence (use ONNX RNN as a fixed-shape cumulative ReLU scan)

Status: current

When to apply. A solver needs a short cumulative recurrence over a static sequence axis, but Loop and Scan are banned and an unrolled chain or dense prefix matrix costs too much. The recurrence must fit a small hidden state and must have statically known sequence length and hidden size.

Recipe. Use RNN with activations=["Relu"], a tiny W/R pair, and a static initial hidden state. Encode the per-step inputs as a sequence tensor, choose hidden channels as the running state, and feed the final or full output into the direct renderer. Treat it as a compact fixed recurrence primitive, not as a dynamic loop.

Why. RNN stores the recurrence weights as small initializers and the hidden-size/activation as attributes. For small state machines this can beat explicit prefix-sum tables, repeated Where/Add/Max chains, or large generator-fitted selector matrices while staying statically shaped.

Tasks. task138 from the 2026-07-04 confirmed archive uses two RNN nodes with ReLU activations: one 3-state recurrence for endpoint/feature selection and one 5-state recurrence for the height/width basis that feeds the final direct Einsum. The promoted graph drops cost 2505 -> 2300, improving score 17.1740 -> 17.2593.

I changed prompts all the time testing which work better, by default I started with 3 prompts:

  1. General prompt
  2. Transfer techniques from similar tasks
  3. Target all remaining opportunities Then I kept sending follow-up prompts until there were 2-3 iterations without improvement and then I stopped working on the task.

For most of the time my agents worked on python ONNX builders not directly on ONNX files because in early stage that gave better results and it was easier to keep track of changes / include solution description / changelog directly in python file. My intuition was that LLMs deal better with python code than raw ONNX files. I later returned to working on ONNX files mostly because our HF space stored ONNX files. I still don't know which was actually better and if it actually makes a difference.

I did some interactive work everyday to get better intuition and see what works / what doesn't work. It definitely helped plan the work for agents better.

Didn't work / underexplored:

  • using bruteforce searches to improve solutions: turned out ineffective so I stopped using it
  • ChatGPT 5.6 Sol Pro: 90% sessions ended with "Thinking Failed" after 2h, when competition ended the same exact prompts worked :(
  • Fable 5: found some improvements but wasn't efficient compared to ChatGPT 5.5

One of the funniest mistakes I made in early stage was that I somehow put all generator files inside repository but forgot about common.py so my agent hallucinated this file making a couple of mistakes. It took me a couple of days to realize that.

Geremie’s work

Skills used: here

  • Started with Qgentic-AI but hit financial constraints
  • Claude Code never worked, it gives up way too easily and said this is the limit (even on a 16.xx task001 solution)
  • Used Codex 5.5 xhigh for 1 month then realised I was losing capabilities by not using Pro (Pro does not exist in Codex)
  • Switched to ChatGPT Web, did it manually for the first day, it was so painful. So I built my own Claude Code skill which uses Chrome to prompt ChatGPT on the web and download ONNXes instead.
  • Optimize 1 task at a time
  • I forced a zero-memory einsum in my ChatGPT prompt so that the AI doesn't try to narrow down the search space (which it is very bad in doing). It just fully focuses on the strategy.
  • Additionally, a 24/7 Codex goal session sweeps through our best ONNXes and tries to re-order einsums so they could run faster.
  • Agent findings, edge cases, techniques, existing hidden-zero cases are all documented in TRICKS.md file for future iterations. Existing failures are NOT used, most of the time it is because the agent under-explored not because that technique was a dead end.
  • Cleanup: if a trick hasn't been used for 14 days, Codex deletes it
  • I used 10 rounds for each ChatGPT sessions. Sometimes, I manually prompt Claude "if after 3 rounds show no improvement, prompt ChatGPT to do a aggressive rewrite"

There is a catch, EinSums in ONNX can only have up to 52 variables. I noticed the agent stumbled because it tried to represent it in more than 52. To mitigate that and still solve the task with an EinSum, I asked it to split into two EinSums with a small intermediate (mostly 4, 8, 16 memory)

I = Einsum("nchw->", input) # its redundant unless my full EinSum uses all 52 variables
final = Einsum(I, ...)

This is an example of my TRICKS.md entry

## `repeated-power-homotopy-factorization` (replace a dense Einsum core with one tied factor reused as powers)
**Status:** current
**Last used:** 2026-07-10 15:58

**Trick.** When an `Einsum` is stuck on a small dense core, try a non-equivalent sign-feasible tied-power factorization such as `B[a,b,c,d] = sum_t C[t,a,b] * C[t,c,d]^2`: repeated reads of `C` are free, so task001 replaced `B[2,2,2,2]` (16 params) with `C[3,2,2]` (12). Do not rely only on random direct fitting; prefit `C` to the passing dense `B`, then homotopy `(1-alpha)*B + alpha*B_factored` from `alpha=0` to `1` with joint retuning, checkpoint/backtracking, and sign-margin validation. If the fused equation runs out of Einsum letters, use repeated-label diagonal/trace ties (task001: `B[g,z,R,S] -> B[g,z,z,z]`) to free labels. This algebraic solver is input-dependent and order-independent unless the surrounding graph already uses an order-dependent RNG/LUT route.

Jin Niu's Work

Optimization Workflow

ChatGPT Pro/Extra High was used for per-task analysis and structural search, while scores, the official audit, exact outputs, convolution bias shapes, runtime, and file hashes were checked locally with Codex. A shared project source provided task data, current best models, tools, constraints, and experiment notes, and was updated with validated improvements and reusable lessons for later tasks.

Low-Cost ONNX Model Design

Optimization focused on initializer parameters and materialized intermediate tensors rather than treating file size or node count as the objective. The dominant-cost subgraph was identified first. Local improvements included removing redundant adapters, narrowing data types, reducing intermediate spatial dimensions, changing Einsum contraction order, fusing encoding and rendering stages, and synthesizing constants from factors already present in the graph. When these changes were insufficient, replacing the representation was usually more effective than deleting a few additional nodes.

The central design question was whether the output could be reconstructed exactly from a small set of low-dimensional variables. The following representation families were explored:

  • Few-node formulas and low-rank synthesis: Direct formulas and compact Einsum contractions generated outputs from coordinates, input summaries, and small factors.
  • Projection, record, and reconstruction: Row or column profiles, endpoints, bounding boxes, and short records retained only the information needed to rebuild a grid.
  • Object-centric and ROI representations: Objects and candidate regions were encoded by position, size, color, and relationships before matching, sorting, or local rendering.
  • Parameter-free spatial transformations: Pool, Resize, DepthToSpace, ConvTranspose, and MaxUnpool sampled, resized, repeated, or rearranged regions using operator attributes instead of large constants.
  • Bit-plane and integer computation: Colors, masks, and states were represented as bit planes, integer codes, or shared bases and decoded only at the output.
  • Convolutional and morphological computation: Conv, QLinearConv, and ConvTranspose expressed neighborhood propagation, boundaries, dilation, and template matching; some tasks used an input patch as a dynamic kernel.
  • Base grid with sparse residuals: The model reused an input or background grid and represented only the cells, colors, or patches that changed.
  • Numeric gating and fused decoding: Signs, ranges, rankings, and attribute-based nonlinearities replaced branches and sometimes combined selection with output generation in one operator.
  • Graph and compiler optimization: Shared-factor extraction, constant synthesis, contraction fusion, common subexpression elimination, output-stage fusion, and data-layout rearrangement reduced cost without changing semantics.

To avoid local optima, candidates were generated from genuinely different representation families rather than as cosmetic variations of the current best graph. ARC-GEN rules were treated as supporting evidence rather than the only interpretation of a task. When local compression stopped producing meaningful gains, major modules or the full representation could be rebuilt. Candidates were compared using exact validation, official cost, and controlled runtime measurements.

Cross-Task Transfer

For each task, both semantic neighbors and ONNX graph-structure neighbors were considered. Semantic neighbors helped interpret transformations, while structural neighbors suggested local techniques such as initializer factorization, smaller intermediate tensors, output-stage fusion, and operator reordering. Entire graphs were not copied blindly. Instead, each technique was transferred only when its assumptions matched the new task, and both successful and unsuccessful experiments were recorded as short, actionable conclusions.

A Less Effective Approach

A general-purpose solver_search project was also explored, combining rule induction, candidate generation, graph compression, official auditing, correctness validation, and experimental feedback. Manual screening was reduced and many semantically correct rules were found, but the generic lowering often remained too expensive. Because the strongest representation was highly task-specific, this solver rarely outperformed models that had been optimized deeply for one task.

Yuichiro’s Work

Seed Cracking

The public ARC-GEN samples were generated using consecutive integer seeds starting at 2025. This led me to hypothesize that the hidden samples followed a similar scheme, using short ranges of consecutive seeds beginning at an unknown base_seed. I ultimately identified it as 33550336, the fifth perfect number, through the following process.

When a submission failed, the server could return one of two distinguishable error messages:

  1. Error processing onnx networks for tasks: [<ids>]: Commonly triggered by a data-dependent out-of-bounds Gather.
  2. Scoring session had non-zero exit code: Commonly triggered by integer division or modulo by zero.

I used these two failure modes as a one-bit communication channel to recover the first hidden input of a single task. After 30 submissions, I had reconstructed the complete input. I then searched locally for seeds that reproduced it and identified 33550336 as the candidate base_seed. I validated this candidate on several other tasks by confirming, through targeted LB probes, that their first hidden samples matched the inputs generated from the same seed.

I next determined the upper end of the hidden seed range for some tasks. I constructed a graph that encoded seeds within a candidate range into the score. To do this, I assigned an artificially small static value_info shape to a node and allowed its actual output shape to increase with the seed, causing larger seeds to produce lower scores. Since the task score was the minimum across all evaluated samples, the observed score revealed the largest hidden seed.

Memorization

Building on the information obtained through seed cracking, we developed highly memorization-based solutions for some tasks. Before using these techniques, we contacted the competition host and received confirmation that such solutions were eligible for scoring.

We mainly used two forms of memorization:

  • Input-fingerprint memorization. We computed a compact fingerprint of each input, identified the corresponding known sample, and selected a stored output or compressed output payload.
  • Evaluation-order memorization. ONNX random operators produced a deterministic, stateful sequence across successive evaluations within the same inference session. We used each evaluation-specific random value to select or reconstruct the corresponding answer, either directly or through compact metadata such as output dimensions, colors, and row masks. This technique depended on the exact evaluation order, a single persistent session, and the runtime’s particular random-number behavior.

Memorization was particularly effective for complex tasks, such as task319, and tasks with very small outputs, such as task048, whose output consisted of a single cell. Those exact two tasks were also hardcoded by some teams in Codegolf competition!

Interestingly, more than half of the tasks for which we used memorization-based solutions still scored lower than the corresponding solutions from the first-place team. Memorization was useful on some tasks, but it was by no means universally superior to generic solutions.

Vu’s work

From early on in the competition, I focused on two things:

  • Local evaluation to match the LB scores. The motivation is simple: we can iterate locally faster if we don’t have to submit to LB for verification. Furthermore, keeping LB submissions low will help our team to be more flexible for team mergers.
  • A platform for collaboration. Unlike traditional Kaggle competitions, I anticipated this competition to be more chaotic, with each team member operating dozens of LLM agents. Just a git repo is not the right way to collaborate.

Evaluation

Ensuring ONNX versions to match is the first step, but there are a few much more annoying problems:

  • Solution pass locally, but getting 0.0 points on the LB. The root cause is failing hidden test samples. To minimize this issue, we add 70 freshly generated ARC-GEN samples per task for offline testing. We still get around 5 to 10 “0.0 points” tasks contaminating our best submission every day. We keep a database of solution candidates, and keep a “Kaggle verified” flag for each entry that was submitted to Kaggle either individually or in a bundle, and has the local CV matching LB. If any time we notice CV and LB not matching, the tasks without that flag is the main suspect. Later on, after the seed has been cracked, we just replaced the randomly generated ARC-GEN with the ones generated with the identified seed. That largely reduced the occurrences of the "0.0 points" issue.
  • Solution evaluates on Kaggle, but getting 0.0 when submitted in a bundle of other tasks. This is a harder CV/LB mismatch to catch. The main culprit is usually a generic class of issue that can be described as “convolution bias size is smaller than number of channels”. We strengthened our evaluator to catch such cases with static analysis.
  • Large EinSums crashing local compute. Sometimes, an EinSum can explode into tens of gigabytes, even hundreds, of RAM. We don’t want to discard any large EinSums, because we learned early on that they can be optimized later by re-ordering the EinSum tensors. Especially for our submission server, where agents submit tens of tasks per minute, this became a large issue. Solution: use Modal. Each solution now is evaluated on its own Modal instance, with as much memory that it wants for as long as it needs, in an isolated container.

Our teammates Yuichiro and Jin Niu later noticed that parallelization can make evaluation incorrect for a few tasks sensitive to float32 precision (because parallelization might enforce a different order of operations).

Collaboration website

The website is pretty simple. We keep a database of solution entries. We keep evaluation time and other stats per task. We also had a separate table to track “unsafe tasks” (not passing all fresh ARC-GEN, but can potentially score well on the LB), “slow tasks” (to isolate the large EinSums). We have a CLI tool and MCP tool for our local agents to interact with the website. We also have a tool to construct a partial submission with task ranges (e.g. “1,3-100,224-250”) and send to Kaggle, all in one click. This makes it easier to do a sanity check like “1-200” (submit all tasks from 1 to 200) few times per day to catch “0.0 points” tasks, while hiding our true score.

We hosted it as a HuggingFace space due to 2 reasons: deployment simplicity and built-in authentication. We later regretted this decision on multiple occasions, as HF infrastructure was proven to be unreliable and caused multiple website and storage failures, especially in the last week of the competition.

The entire team had access to maintain the space in case of any outages/bugs. And yeah, vibe coded software indeed has lots of bugs.

Important lesson: never rely on HuggingFace for your critical infrastructure and data!

Funniest part of our website, in my opinion, is the “discussions” page, where our agents can write discussion posts, read previous posts, and comment on each-other’s posts. Screenshot of Geremie’s agents spamming:

Problem solving

My workflow is pretty similar to everyone else’s workflows in this competition. I started with Claude Code, but after reaching 6900 at the beginning of this competition and looking at my usage bill, I realized Claude is terrible for this job.

I use GPT Pro in browser for problem solving. Copy-pasting was too time-consuming and dumb for my liking, so like Geremie, I also used Claude Code with Browser extension to manage all the GPT sessions. I keep a list of common tricks, distilled from the website discussion posts, so my agents can read the digest before starting a new solve. Later on, I incorporated Jacek “TECHNIQUES.md” as the main driver. One of the most successful tricks in pair-golfing (solving task together with the agent) is: "/goal taskXXX looks similar to taskYYY, which scored 2 points higher, please golf taskXXX to that score".

Bonus: task359, memory=0, params=1, score=25

def _const(name: str, value: np.ndarray) -> onnx.TensorProto:
    return numpy_helper.from_array(np.asarray(value), name=name)


def make_onnx() -> onnx.ModelProto:
    inits = [
        _const('scale', np.array([1.2599999643365771e-14], dtype=np.float32)),
    ]
    nodes = [
        helper.make_node('Einsum', ['scale', 'scale', 'input', 'input', 'input', 'input', 'input', 'input', 'input', 'input', 'input',
 'input', 'input', 'input', 'input', 'input', 'input', 'input', 'input', 'input', 'input', 'input',
 'scale', 'scale'], ['output'], name='output', equation='S,S,Bahl,Baml,Bahp,Bomn,Bepn,Bepw,Beqw,Bgxw,Bgvw,Bgvu,Bohu,Botu,Bfts,Bfhs,Bchi,Bcji,Bojk,Bchr,Bdrk,Bdrw,S,S->Bohw'),
    ]
    graph = helper.make_graph(
        nodes,
        'g',
        [
            helper.make_tensor_value_info('input', 1, [1, 10, 30, 30]),
        ],
        [
            helper.make_tensor_value_info('output', 1, [1, 10, 30, 30]),
        ],
        inits,
        value_info=[
        ],
    )
    model = helper.make_model(
        graph,
        opset_imports=[
            helper.make_opsetid('', 12),
        ],
        producer_name='',
    )
    model.ir_version = 10
    onnx.checker.check_model(model, full_check=True)
    return model
